title: Persepolis: the animal capitals and the 1971 celebrations
standfirst: Two centuries of ruins, one very public party, and a design motif that returns on objects.
metaDescription: What the double-animal column capitals of Persepolis are, and how the site was used for the 1971 celebrations of 2,500 years of Iranian monarchy.

body.text: The distinctive Achaemenid "Persepolitan" column has a base, a fluted shaft and a double-animal capital, mostly bulls, carved back to back; the animals project from the column and function as brackets for the roof timbers [@wp-column]. Lions, man-headed bulls and griffins also occur [@wp-column]. [UPGRADE: cite Schmidt, *Persepolis I* (OIP 68, 1953) by page after opening it; the Wikipedia citation is a pointer only [@schmidt1953].]
UNESCO inscribed Persepolis on its World Heritage List in 1979 [@unesco114].

In October 1971 celebrations were held at Persepolis to mark what was presented as 2,500 years of monarchy and the twenty-fifth centennial of Cyrus's empire; they opened on 12 October [@loc19; @wp-2500]. The Library of Congress records that the ceremonies drew adverse domestic comment, that honoured guests were foreign heads of state, and that Khomeini condemned them in a widely circulated declaration [@loc19].

The only freely licensed picture we have verified for this piece is a modern photograph of the Apadana columns (CC BY-SA 4.0, Bernard Gagnon). Contemporary photographs of the 1971 "Tent City" are on hold pending a rights check (see RIGHTS-AUDIT.md).
